title: A case of tumor-like inflammatory demyelinating disease with progressive brain and spinal cord involvement
case_prompt:
A 24-year-old right-handed man presented with 2 days of severe headache and incoherent speech. Two weeks earlier he had a cold with cough and fever that resolved one week before admission. He had no significant past medical or family history and took no medications.  
Vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination showed cognitive impairment, neck rigidity, and a positive Kernig’s sign; Brudzinski’s signs were negative.  
Laboratory tests revealed normal blood counts, liver and renal function, electrolytes, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Autoimmune antibodies and serologies for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B and C were negative.  
CSF analysis showed an opening pressure of 250 mmH₂O (normal <180), protein of 51 mg/dl (normal <40), normal cell counts, glucose, and chloride; Gram stain and bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures were negative; the IgG index was normal without oligoclonal bands.  
An EEG showed diffuse intermittent slow waves over the left temporal area; visual and brainstem auditory evoked potentials were normal.  
Brain MRI revealed a 5-cm irregular mass in the left basal ganglia with T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement, and surrounding edema. Proton MR spectroscopy demonstrated an elevated choline peak and a suppressed N-acetylaspartate peak. Spinal MRI was unremarkable.  
He was treated with IV dexamethasone (10 mg/day) and IV acyclovir (500 mg every 8 hours) for 1 week, but his headache and cognitive impairment worsened.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious causes ruled out — “Gram staining and bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial cultures on the CSF were negative.”  
2. Multiple sclerosis considered less likely — “The immunoglobulin G (IgG) index was normal without oligoclonal bands.”  
3. Demyelinating lesion was initially favored — “In view of the case history and complementary examinations, the diagnosis of a demyelinating lesion was considered.”  
4. Intracranial tumor remained in the differential — “The differential diagnosis included brain demyelinating disease and brain tumor.”  
5. Low-grade glioma was suspected after steroid failure and MRI enhancement — “Because of non-response to corticosteroid therapy and contrast enhancement on MRI, a low-grade glioma was suspected.”
